query: For transition-metal catalysts, formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis explaining what governs catalytic activity, selectivity, or durability and why. Specify an unnamed controlled comparison that would reveal the governing cause, the observations predicted relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, supporting prior evidence, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In transition‐metal catalysts, a synergistic interplay between remotely located (subsurface) alloying atoms and controlled surface strain adjusts the d‐band electronic structure of surface active sites, thereby fine‐tuning the adsorption energies of key reaction intermediates and governing both the activity and selectivity of catalytic reactions.
generation.material_initial_state: Nanoparticles of a primary transition metal catalyst (e.g., pure Cu or PdAg) with well‐defined crystalline facets but without intentional subsurface dopants or engineered strain.
generation.intervention: Introduce a small fraction of a secondary metal (e.g., Pt) that preferentially locates in subsurface positions together with applying controlled surface strain (via nanoparticle shape/composition control) to modify the surface electronic properties.
generation.conditions: Catalytic reactions performed under conditions similar to those in hydrogenation or oxidation reactions (e.g., ambient to moderate temperatures and pressures) where intermediate adsorption strength is critical; experiments conducted on nanoparticles where alloying and strain can be accurately controlled.
generation.structural_mediator: A modified d‐band structure of the surface atoms—specifically a downward shift of the d‐band center due to ligand effects from subsurface dopants combined with strain‐induced alterations—mediates the optimal adsorption energies of reactive intermediates.
generation.mechanism: Remote dopants, although not exposed at the surface, alter the electronic density of surface atoms via extended orbital interactions, while controlled tensile or compressive strain further adjusts the d‐band center. This dual modification tailors the adsorption strengths of species (e.g., hydrogen, oxygenated intermediates), striking a balance between too weak and too strong binding, which in turn enhances catalytic turnover and selectivity.
generation.predicted_outcome: Catalysts engineered with both subsurface alloying (e.g., dilute Pt in a Cu matrix) and controlled low surface strain (e.g., ~0.3% strain) will exhibit a moderate d‐band center shift leading to improved turnover frequencies and higher selectivities (for example, in the selective hydrogenation of unsaturated aldehydes or in lowering overpotentials for oxidation reactions) compared to catalysts without these modifications.
generation.baseline: Catalysts composed solely of the primary transition metal (without subsurface dopants or deliberate strain engineering) which exhibit less optimal adsorption energy profiles and consequently lower catalytic activity or selectivity.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to apply primarily to nanoscale transition‐metal catalysts where both the alloying (remote dopant distribution) and surface strain can be finely manipulated; its validity may be limited in bulk materials or systems dominated by strong support interactions.
generation.uncertainty: The individual effects of remote alloying (as seen in dilute Pt in Cu systems, PMC11075014) and surface strain (as demonstrated in Pd@PdAg nanocrystals, PMC9419203) have been observed independently. However, the quantitative interplay between these two effects and their combined impact on intermediate adsorption energies remains uncertain and requires further systematic evaluation.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of nanoparticle catalysts: (A) one with a small amount of Pt intentionally introduced so that the Pt atoms preferentially occupy subsurface positions in a Cu (or PdAg) matrix along with engineered low surface strain, and (B) a control set with the identical overall elemental composition but with the Pt forced to remain absent from subsurface sites or with higher, uncontrolled strain. Perform a catalytic reaction sensitive to intermediate adsorption energies (e.g., the selective hydrogenation of an unsaturated aldehyde).
measurements: Determine the d‐band center via X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) or X-ray absorption near-edge spectroscopy (XANES).
Measure intermediate adsorption strengths using in situ spectroscopies (e.g., infrared absorption) or temperature-programmed desorption studies.
Quantify catalytic activity and selectivity via reaction rate measurements and product distribution analysis (e.g., using gas chromatography).
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the catalyst from set (A) does not exhibit a statistically significant downward shift in the d‐band center, improved intermediate adsorption energies, and enhanced catalytic activity/selectivity relative to control set (B), or if variations in subsurface dopant location and surface strain do not correlate with predictable changes in performance, then the mechanistic hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractWith heterogeneous catalysts, chemical promotion takes place at their surfaces. Even in the case of single-atom alloys, where small quantities of a reactive metal are dispersed within the main host, it is assumed that both elements are exposed and available to bond with the reactants. Here, we show, on the basis of in situ X-ray absorption spectroscopy data, that in alloy catalysts made from Pt highly diluted in Cu the Pt atoms are located at the inner interface between the metal nanoparticles and the silica support instead. Kinetic experiments indicated that these catalysts still display better selectivity for the hydrogenation of unsaturated aldehydes to unsaturated alcohols than the pure metals. Density functional theory calculations corroborated the stability of Pt at the metal–support interface and explained the catalytic performance as being due to a remote lowering of the activation barrier for the dissociation of H2 at Cu sites by the internal Pt atoms.Keywords: single-atom alloy (SAA) catalysts; in situ studies; X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS, XANES, EXAFS); density functional theory (DFT); infrared absorption spectroscopy (IR); segregation; diffusion; hydrogen

AbstractThe strain effect is a critical knob to tune the catalytic performance and has received unprecedented research interest recently. However, it is difficult to distinguish the strain effect from the synergistic effect, especially in alloyed catalysts. Here we have synthesized Pd@PdAg icosahedra and {111} truncated bi-pyramids with only different surface strains between them as electrocatalysts for the ethanol oxidation reaction (EOR). Due to the same exposed facets and compositions of the two electrocatalysts, their EOR performances are mainly determined by the surface strains of PdAg alloys. These two electrocatalysts provide a perfect model to investigate the role of the strain effect in tuning the EOR performance. It is indicated that Pd@PdAg {111} truncated bi-pyramids with a surface strain of 0.3% show better catalytic activity and durability than Pd@PdAg icosahedra with a surface strain of 2.1% including commercial Pd/C.
